newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Growing prosperity threatens Asian authoritarianism.
newsitem.headline: Growing prosperity threatens Asian authoritarianism.

text.p: When the United States issued its first report on human rights abuses world-wide 20 years ago, there was little to celebrate in Asia.
Martial law gripped the Philippines and Taiwan. South Korea's generals brooked no opposition to their iron rule.
Pol Pot's twisted ideology was fertilising the rice paddies of Cambodia with human blood. Communism was sweeping south through Vietnam, igniting a exodus of boatpeople fleeing on rickety boats.
China was an enigma. Mao was dead but the bamboo curtain remained firmly down and double-locked.
Two decades later, the latest report found no shortage of abuse. But there were far fewer names on the list.
The State Department report on 193 countries pointed the finger at China, Burma and North Korea as the blackest spots.
The report said violence against women was a serious problem in South Korea, and called Vietnam's record poor.

It accused Burma's military regime, the State Law and Order Council (SLORC), of severe repression which "increased during 1996, even as increased economic activity fostered the appearance of greater normalcy.
"Out of sight of most visitors, citizens continued to live subject at any time and without appeal to the arbitrary and sometimes brutal dictates of the military dictatorship."
Burma's hardline rulers predictably hit back, accusing the United States of spreading "nonsense" and engaging in a conspiracy against the Southeast Asian nation.
Indonesia was mum on East Timor, but South Korea was chastened.
"It's true South Korea has been traditionally discriminating against women," said an official at the Ministry of Political Affairs in charge of women's issues.
"But the government is trying to do away with discrimination and violence against women by introducing tougher regulations."
Such a statement would have been unthinkable from Seoul even a decade ago.
But as standards of living rose steadily in Asia, so have demands for greater self-determination.
The newly-emerging middle classes of the Philippines, Thailand, South Korea and Taiwan have seized the day, prising open the fist of authoritarian government.

People power in the streets of Manila swept Ferdinand Marcos into exile in 1986. A decade ago, in 1987, the South Korean middle classes took to the streets forcing strongman President Chun Doo Hwan to concede presidential elections.
Taiwan lifted martial law the same year and ended 43 years of emergency rule in 1991.

Burma reacted violently to the groundswell of emotion sweeping through Asia, brutually cracking down on student demonstrators in Rangoon in 1988, a foretaste of things to come around Beijing's Tiananmen Square a year later in 1989.
But Burma's SLORC has proved powerless to silence the quiet tones of a soft-spoken woman. Aung San Sui Kyi continues to draw crowds to her speeches, defying the military leaders.
China has been more successful in purging opposition voices. The State Department report concluded that "no dissidents were known to be active (in China) at year's end".

The report was of keen interest in the British colony of Hong Kong which is reeling under Beijing's threats to dilute its civil liberties laws, including a Bill of Rights, when it resumes control of the British colony in the middle of the year.
More than a century and a half of British rule ends when sovereignty of Hong Kong reverts to China at midnight on June 30, now 151 days away.

Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement fears Beijing will gradually snuff out freedoms enjoyed in the freewheeling community of six million people despite promises to permit their capitalist way of life to continue unabated for 50 years.
"Human rights will deteriorate after July 1," concluded pro-democracy activist Szeto Wah on Friday.

He regards China's proposals to strike out key clauses on civil liberties as a dire omen. "If they don't have any intention of cracking down in Hong Kong then why are they wanting to revise the laws?"
But China may find Hong Kong a hard nut to crack. Hong Kong is a westernised, wealthy, well-travelled community which relishes the good things money and freedom has brought.
Szeto and his allies in Hong Kong's democracy movement have no intention of bowing out gracefully.
"We are psychologically and practically prepared," he said. "Hong Kong people have never had to pay a price for their freedoms. If they want them to continue they will have to pay the price."
